entities.name: Ticonderoga-class cruiser
entities.label: Text
entities.summary:
The Ticonderoga-class cruiser, launched in the early 1980s, represents a significant advancement in naval warfare technology, specifically in guided missile systems. These cruisers were designed to enhance the United States Navy's capabilities during the Cold War, allowing for multi-role missions that included air defense, anti-submarine warfare, and land attack operations. The class was named after Fort Ticonderoga, a landmark of American Revolutionary War history, and has played a pivotal role in demonstrating the evolution of naval power in the late 20th century.

Commissioned between 1983 and 1994, the Ticonderoga-class cruisers were equipped with the Aegis Combat System, a groundbreaking integrated naval weapons system that included advanced radar and missile capabilities. These vessels, with a displacement of around 9,600 tons, could carry up to 122 missiles, including Tomahawk cruise missiles, which were pivotal during conflicts such as the Gulf War in 1991. The ability to engage multiple targets simultaneously made the Ticonderoga-class a formidable deterrent against potential threats, fundamentally altering naval engagement strategies.

The legacy of the Ticonderoga-class cruisers has been profound, influencing naval design and strategy globally. They set a standard for future warships, with their design principles being adopted by several other nations. As of the early 2020s, many Ticonderoga-class ships remain operational, showcasing their lasting impact on naval architecture and combat effectiveness. The class serves as a reminder of a pivotal era in military history, highlighting how advancements in technology can redefine warfare.
